newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma rejects spending cuts, govt pushes on.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma rejects spending cuts, govt pushes on.

text.p: Russia's reformist government said on Monday it had laid the foundations for economic growth during its first 100 days in power but its parliamentary foes, unimpressed, rejected its plan to cut spending.

Ministers vowed to press on with the cuts regardless after the blow from the communist-led lower house of parliament, which threw out both its proposal to slash spending under this year's budget and a parliamentary plan for less drastic cuts.
"What can you do? It happens with everybody," was all First Deputy Boris Nemtsov had to say when he heard about the votes in the State Duma.

Many Duma deputies fear the cuts will hit their electorate, made up mainly of the millions whose wages, pensions and other benefits, eaten by inflation at the start of the transition from communism, have recently been paid with big delays -- if at all.
Minutes earlier Nemtsov, one of the new government's young turks, had said the cabinet had brought parliament around to some of its reforms, notably a new tax code last week.

At a news conference given 99 days after he took up his post, Nemtsov said the cabinet was on track towards ending two years of pension delays, had brought down inflation and interest rates and made a start in tackling widespread corruption.
"Furthermore, we consider that in those 100 days the basis has been laid for economic growth," he said, adding that the growth itself would probably not come until next year.
He also announced a cut in electricity prices for companies that paid their bills on time, following a similar move on gas prices last year.
But he admitted that the government had quite a way to go towards getting wages paid on time.

Commenting on the first major scandal to hit the new cabinet, he said an investigation had been launched after a newspaper published pictures it said were of Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov in a sauna with several naked women.
Kovalyov was at work on Monday, officials said, despite asking to be suspended to give him time to clear his name.
"The state has no right to climb into bed with the people, it has absolutely no right, and one would hope it would be the same the other way around," Nemtsov said.

Nemtsov, 37, seen by some as a would-be president, responded to new concerns over Boris Yeltsin's health by saying the Kremlin leader had "risen like a phoenix" from the ashes since last year, when he underwent open heart surgery.

Yeltsin missed a late-night gala concert on Saturday night during a summit with leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial democracies but aides said he was just tired and Nemtsov said he had recovered by the time he met him on Monday.
"All the delegates looked tired, only the president looked cheery and fresh and he asked me to report on what happened in the country in the past few days," Nemtsov said.
Yeltsin won a strong endorsement of his policies from the G7, whose three-day summit helped deepen Russia's integration into the capitalist world's main economic institutions.
But at home, the tussle between government and parliament over economic policy appeared to be going parliament's way.

Deputies voted by 210 votes to 112 to throw out the cabinet plan to cut 108 trillion roubles ($18.8 billion) from spending and rejected by 195 to 137 a proposal by one of their communist colleagues for 39 trillion roubles of cuts, or "sequester".
The government has said that, with or without the support of the Duma, which starts its summer recess on Tuesday, the state is simply unable to pay its bills.

"Today and tomorrow we will have consultations with all the parties," Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov told reporters after the vote. Asked what it would do if parliament did not agree he said: "We will go ahead with the sequester."
"The only trouble is that when it comes to reporting on the budget they will blame us for not adhering to the budget law."
